extracted.intended_audience: patent applicants, practitioners, and USPTO examiners
extracted.subtask_short: petition to revive abandoned patent application
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for filing and evaluating petitions under 37 CFR 1.137 to revive abandoned U.S. patent (including provisional) applications, and related procedural requirements (timing, burden of proof, terminal disclaimers, access to files, publications).

rubrics_metrics.name: Standard for 'unavoidable' delay
rubrics_metrics.description: A petition under 37 CFR 1.137(a) requires a showing to the satisfaction of the Commissioner that the entire delay in filing the required reply from the due date for the reply until the filing of a grantable petition pursuant to 37 CFR 1.137(a) was unavoidable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decisions on revival are made on a case-by-case basis. The petitioner carries the burden of proof. Delay resulting from lack of knowledge or improper application of the patent statute, rules of practice or the MPEP does not constitute 'unavoidable' delay. Examples: simply permitting the maximum extendable period to expire while awaiting a notice of allowance is not 'unavoidable'; failure to file papers/fees in compliance with 37 CFR 1.8/1.10 is not 'unavoidable'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clerical/employee error may establish 'unavoidable' delay (three-part test)
rubrics_metrics.description: A delay resulting from an error on the part of an employee in performing a clerical function may provide the basis for showing 'unavoidable' delay, provided it is shown that: (A) the error was the cause of the delay at issue; (B) there was in place a business routine for performing the clerical function that could reasonably be relied upon to avoid errors; and (C) the employee was sufficiently trained and experienced with regard to the function and routine so that reliance upon such employee represented the exercise of due care.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cite In re Egbers, In re Katrapat. The three conditions must be demonstrated in the petition; mere assertion of an employee error without evidence of routines and training is insufficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proper notification of change of correspondence address required
rubrics_metrics.description: An adequate showing of 'unavoidable' delay resulting from mailing to an old uncorrected address requires a showing that due care was taken to adhere to the requirement for prompt notification in each concerned application and must include an adequate showing that a timely notification of the change of address was filed in the application concerned and in a manner reasonably calculated to call attention to the fact that it was a notification of a change of address.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The following do not constitute proper notification: (A) mere inclusion of a different address in a paper filed for another purpose without mention of an address change; (B) notification on a paper listing plural applications as being affected (except under Customer Number practice — MPEP §403); (C) lack of notification or belated notification to the USPTO. Applicants should file address-change papers promptly in each application (see MPEP §§402, 601.03).

rubrics_metrics.name: Deliberate/intentional abandonment or delay precludes relief
rubrics_metrics.description: Abandonment considered a deliberately chosen course of action cannot be 'unintentional' within 37 CFR 1.137(b), and an intentional delay in seeking revival precludes finding of unavoidable or unintentional delay.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Intentional delay is not cured by correctness of prior decisions or subsequent discovery of information. Example: delaying revival until industry or competitor interest appears is the antithesis of 'unavoidable'/'unintentional'. See Application of G and Maldague. The Office views deliberate deferral unfavorably; petitions filed after deliberate inaction will be denied.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement to show delay was unavoidable/unintentional until petition filing
rubrics_metrics.description: 35 U.S.C. 133 and 151 require showing that the 'delay' was 'unavoidable,' which requires not only showing the delay that resulted in abandonment was unavoidable but also a showing of unavoidable delay until the filing of a petition to revive. Applicant must cause a petition under 37 CFR 1.137(a) to be filed without delay (promptly upon becoming notified or otherwise becoming aware of abandonment).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failure to file promptly after awareness undermines ability to show the entire delay was unavoidable. Removal of the word 'promptly' from the regulation does not permit deliberate delay. See In re Application of Takao and Application of S (denial where petitioner deliberately deferred filing).

rubrics_metrics.name: Timing thresholds and evidentiary expectations (3 months / 1 year rules)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Office generally will not question intentional delay when a petition is filed (1) within 3 months of the date the applicant is first notified that the application is abandoned; and (2) within 1 year of the date of abandonment. If not filed within 3 months, the Office will require a showing how the delay was 'unavoidable' (for 1.137(a)) or may require further information about how the delay was 'unintentional' (for 1.137(b)). If not filed within 1 year, the Office will require further information about when the applicant first became aware of abandonment and how discovery occurred despite due care.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applicants are advised to file within 3 months of first notification to avoid questions of intentional delay. When filing outside these windows, include thorough factual showings (dates, explanation of diligence) to expedite consideration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Party whose delay is relevant — who is evaluated
rubrics_metrics.description: Under 37 CFR 1.137 the question is whether the delay by the party having the right or authority to reply to avoid abandonment was unavoidable or unintentional. If the applicant assigned entire right/title/interest to a third party (and retains no legal/equitable interest), the applicant's delay is irrelevant. If a third party controls prosecution (assignee, licensee, etc.), that party's decision binds the applicant unless the contractor acts only in a fiduciary capacity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If prosecution is controlled by a third party under an agreement, the applicant is bound by that third party's actions/inactions unless the contract expressly limits authority to fiduciary-only. Cases: Kim v. Quigg; Winkler v. Ladd; Futures Technology Ltd. v. Quigg.

rubrics_metrics.name: Burden of proof for 1.137(a) and 1.137(b) petitions
rubrics_metrics.description: 37 CFR 1.137(a)(3) requires a showing to the satisfaction of the Commissioner that the entire delay was unavoidable; thus the applicant must carry the burden of proof in every 1.137(a) petition to establish unavoidable delay. 37 CFR 1.137(b)(3) requires a statement that the entire delay was unintentional, but the Commissioner may require additional information and in some cases may require the applicant to carry the burden of proof to establish unintentional delay.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Generally §1.137(b) petitions need only the statement, but the Office may request more if there is a question. Cite Haines; Application of G.

rubrics_metrics.name: Terminal disclaimer requirement for revival petitions
rubrics_metrics.description: 37 CFR 1.137(d) requires that a petition under either 37 CFR 1.137(a) or 1.137(b) be accompanied by a terminal disclaimer (and fee) in: (A) a design application; (B) a nonprovisional utility application filed before June 8, 1995; or (C) a nonprovisional plant application filed before June 8, 1995. The disclaimer must dedicate to the public a terminal part of the patent term equivalent to the applicable period (period of abandonment or other defined period).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The terminal disclaimer is not a substitute for showing unavoidable/unintentional delay. The filing of a terminal disclaimer does not excuse intentional delay. If applicant believes the terminal disclaimer is inappropriate, file a petition under 37 CFR 1.183 requesting waiver for 'extraordinary situation' where 'justice requires' relief (petition fee applies). Forms PTO/SB/62 and PTO/SB/63 may be used; PTO will not indicate the period disclaimed in its revival decision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Request for reconsideration timing and extensions
rubrics_metrics.description: 37 CFR 1.137(e) requires any request for reconsideration or review of a decision refusing to revive an abandoned application or lapsed patent to be filed within 2 months of the decision refusing to revive (or within such time as set in the decision). Unless a decision indicates otherwise, this time period may be extended under 37 CFR 1.136.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A renewed petition, request for reconsideration, or other petition seeking review filed outside the time period may require a specific showing that the entire delay was 'unavoidable' (1.137(a)) or 'unintentional' (1.137(b)). Intentional delays remain inexcusable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Application of 1.137 to provisional applications and 12-month limit
rubrics_metrics.description: 37 CFR 1.137 is applicable to a provisional application abandoned for failure to reply to an Office requirement, and such a petition must be accompanied by any outstanding reply. 35 U.S.C. 111(b)(5) regards a provisional application as abandoned 12 months after filing and not subject to revival after that 12-month period; revival may restore pendency only up to the end of that 12-month period.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: It is permissible to file a petition later than 12 months only to revive the application for the 12-month period following filing. Note extension rules if 12-month anniversary falls on weekend/holiday (pends to next business day).

rubrics_metrics.name: Form availability for petitions and terminal disclaimers
rubrics_metrics.description: Form PTO/SB/61 may be used to file a petition for revival of an unavoidably abandoned application; Forms PTO/SB/62 and PTO/SB/63 may be used when filing a terminal disclaimer in accordance with 37 CFR 1.137(d).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the specified forms where applicable to ensure compliance and proper processing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examiner's statement when petition to set aside examiner's holding filed
rubrics_metrics.description: 37 CFR 1.181 states the examiner 'may be directed by the Commissioner to furnish a written statement within a specific time setting forth the reasons for his or her decision upon the matters averred in the petition, supplying a copy thereof to the petitioner.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unless requested, such a statement should not be prepared. See MPEP §1002.01 for practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public access to abandoned applications (conditions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Access to an abandoned application may be provided to any person, subject to 37 CFR 1.14(i), if a written request for access is submitted and if the abandoned application is not within the file wrapper of a pending continued prosecution application (CPA) under 37 CFR 1.53(d) and is referred to: (A) in a U.S. patent application publication or patent; (B) in another U.S. application open to public inspection; or (C) in an international application designating the U.S. and published under PCT Article 21(2).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A copy of specification, drawings, and papers relating to the file of an abandoned published application may be provided upon written request and fee (37 CFR 1.19(b)(2)); Form PTO/SB/68 may be used to request access under 37 CFR 1.14(e). See MPEP §103.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedures for pulling and forwarding abandoned application files
rubrics_metrics.description: Files of abandoned applications are pulled and forwarded to the Files Repository on a biweekly basis one month after the full 6-month statutory period has expired; however the date of abandonment is after midnight of the date on which the shortened statutory period, including any 37 CFR 1.136 extensions, expired.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners must carefully scrutinize files to verify abandonment (check for Board decisions with allowed claims). Files are ordered via PALM transaction (input location code, employee number, patent/app numbers); PALM response indicates status (accepted, off-site warehouse, not located, prior request pending, invalid number). Drawings are usually stored within the file wrapper and delivered together.

rubrics_metrics.name: Notifying applicants of abandonment (USPTO practice)
rubrics_metrics.description: Patent Examining Corps mails a Notice of Abandonment form PTOL-1432 to the correspondence address of record in all applications which become abandoned for failure to prosecute; mere failure to receive the notice does not affect the status of the abandoned application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applicants should act promptly after receiving notice—failure to act promptly may preclude relief. If applicant contends Office action or notice not received, consider problems with correspondence address; file change of address papers promptly in each affected application (see MPEP §§402, 601.03). A petition to withdraw the holding of abandonment may be available if reply was mailed with a certificate of mailing (MPEP §512).

rubrics_metrics.name: Abstracts, abbreviatures, and defensive publications — definitions and effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Abstracts and abbreviatures (historical programs) summarized technical disclosures; Defensive Publication Program (Apr 1968–May 8, 1985) published abstracts if applicant waived enforceable patent rights and provisionally abandoned. Defensive publications are publications (not patents or application publications under 35 U.S.C. 122(b)) and are prior art as of their publication date.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Defensive publication could affect entitlement to benefit of earlier filing dates for continuations if the first continuing application was not filed within 30 months. Defensive Publication Abstracts/search copies were provided to application file, Patent Search Room, and examiner search files; files maintained in File Information Unit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Citation and use of abstracts/abbreviatures/defensive publications as prior art
rubrics_metrics.description: Abstracts, abbreviatures, and defensive publications must be referred to as publications; they are cited as prior art under 35 U.S.C. 102(a) or 102(b) effective from their Official Gazette publication date.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See Ex parte Osmond and In re Osmond and MPEP §2136 for precedent and further guidance on use as references.
